summary: Gives an overview of the Handle System, a general-purpose global name service for secured name resolution and administration. It describes the namespace and service architecture and the relationship to DNS, LDAP/X.500 and URNs. Handles are unique names for digital objects and other Internet resources. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Imagine a global phone book where every digital item has a permanent name that always leads to where it lives now, even if it moves. This is a tour of how that system is organized.

questions: why is the handle system different from dns
subtitle: A distributed global name service for persistent identifiers.

tldr.problem: DNS works for host names but was not designed as a general-purpose naming service. Applications need a system where names remain valid even when resources move or change ownership, with per-name administrative control.
tldr.mechanism: The Handle System is a distributed name service where each name (handle) consists of a naming authority prefix and a local name suffix, managed by a Global Handle Registry that dispatches requests to Local Handle Services. Each handle can be assigned multiple values and attributes that are updated as the resource evolves.
tldr.outcome: Applications can use handles as persistent identifiers for digital objects, with centralized management, distributed administration, and security features for authentication and data protection. Early adopters include digital libraries and DOI services.

today: RFC 3650 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. The Handle System remains in use by digital library projects, the DOI Foundation, and other organizations needing persistent identifiers.

sections.title: What the Handle System Does
sections.content:
The Handle System is a distributed global name service, similar in concept to DNS but designed for general-purpose resource naming rather than just host addresses. It manages handles, which are unique, persistent names for digital objects and other Internet resources. Each handle never has to change, even if the object it names moves to a new location or changes ownership. The name persists while the associated information (the current location, contact information, or other attributes) is updated as needed.

The system uses an open protocol, a defined namespace, and a reference implementation. It supports secured name resolution and administration, meaning clients can verify server responses with digital signatures, and administrators can prove their identity before making changes. Each handle can have its own set of administrators independent of system administrators, allowing fine-grained control over who can manage what.
sections.eli5: A handle is a permanent name that points to information about something. Unlike a street address that changes when you move, a handle stays the same forever. You look up a handle and the system tells you where the item is now.

sections.title: Why the Handle System Exists
sections.content:
DNS was built to map domain names to IP addresses for network routing. But as the Internet grew, people wanted to use DNS for other things: naming documents, services, datasets, without risking the performance of core network routing. DNS also requires a network administrator to manage all names at a domain level. There is no way for an individual user or application to own and manage their own names without going through the domain administrator.

URLs (like http://example.com/path/to/file) tie resources to their current location. When a file moves or an organization reorganizes its web server, the URL breaks. The Handle System was designed to overcome these limits by providing a system where any organization can join the global namespace with its own naming authority, administer its own names independently, and reassign locations without breaking the name. Additionally, a single handle can reference multiple instances or attributes of a resource, supporting both high-availability and evolving information models.
sections.eli5: DNS is built for computers to talk to each other, not for naming things people care about. Websites break when they move. Handles don't break because they're designed to stick around.

sections.title: How Handles Are Named
sections.content:
Every handle consists of two parts separated by a forward slash: a naming authority and a local name. For example, 10.1045/january99-bearman has the naming authority 10.1045 (D-Lib Magazine) and the local name january99-bearman (a specific article). Naming authorities are arranged in a hierarchical tree. The naming authority 10 might be the Digital Object Identifier (DOI) project, and 10.1045 a child naming authority for a specific publication. This ensures that any combination of naming authority and local name is globally unique.

Handles support Unicode characters and are encoded in UTF-8 for transmission, allowing names in any language. By default, handles are case-sensitive, but a handle service can choose to treat ASCII characters (A-Z) as case-insensitive. This design allows existing local naming systems to join the Handle System by obtaining a unique naming authority, so a library's local catalogue identifiers can become globally unique and persistent handles.
sections.eli5: A handle is like an address: organization/item-name. The organization part is unique worldwide, and each organization manages its item names. Think of it like NYTimes/article-12345.

sections.title: How the System Is Organized
sections.content:
The Handle System uses a two-tier distributed architecture. At the top is the Global Handle Registry (GHR), a single distributed service that manages naming authorities and directs handle requests to the appropriate service. It maintains records for each naming authority, including where its handles are managed and how to contact that service. Below the GHR are many Local Handle Services (LHS), each hosted by an organization responsible for handles under one or more naming authorities. Each service can replicate across multiple geographic sites, and each site can have multiple servers, so there is no single point of failure and load can be balanced across many computers.

When a client wants to resolve a handle, it first queries the Global Handle Registry with the naming authority part, gets back the address of the responsible Local Handle Service, and then queries that service with the full handle. Clients can cache this service information to avoid repeated trips to the Global Handle Registry. Each handle service stores a set of handle values: a name can resolve to multiple values like URLs, email addresses, or administrative contacts, each with its own access control and time-to-live settings.
sections.eli5: There's one central registry that knows which organization manages each handle prefix. When you look up a handle, you ask the central registry where to find it, then ask that organization's server for the details.

sections.title: Security and Administration
sections.content:
The Handle System supports multiple security features. Clients can request that server responses be digitally signed so they can verify the response came from the real server and has not been tampered with. For sensitive data, clients can establish encrypted sessions with servers using shared session keys. Handle values can be marked with permissions: public-readable, readable only by the administrator, or writable only by the administrator. This allows storing credentials or secret data in the Handle System without exposing it to the public.

Each handle can have one or more administrators, independent from the system administrator. Administrators prove their identity using either a secret key (like a password) or a public key (like a certificate), and the authentication process is a challenge-response protocol to prevent eavesdropping. Different administrators can have different permissions: one might be able to add or remove values, another might manage administrators. This distributed administration model is fundamental to the Handle System's design, allowing large organizations to delegate handle management without centralizing control.
sections.eli5: You can prove you're the owner of a handle before making changes, and you can mark some information as secret. Different people can have different powers to manage a handle.
